title: Fast starters and slow finishers: A large-scale data analysis of pacing at the beginning and end of the marathon for recreational runners
population: Recreational marathon runners from big-city marathons
findings: Analysis of 1.7 million recreational marathon runners, focused on pacing at the start and end of the race.
Starting or finishing too quickly resulted in poorer finish times: fast starts tend to be very fast, leading to later endurance problems, while fast finishes suggest overly cautious early pacing.
Women tend to pace their race more effectively than men, but can be more cautious, costing them minutes overall.
limitations: No effect sizes in the abstract; results/splits only, with no physiology or training history; marathon-specific.
implications: Race-day guidance should include a start-pace cap and discourage a strong finishing kick as a sign of a too-cautious start; no numeric threshold is supported by the abstract.
Model finishing time with a fade term; starting too fast worsens finish time.

verification.notes: Crossref confirmed metadata (J Sports Analytics, 2018-04-24, Smyth); Europe PMC has no record of this DOI, so the abstract was read from the Semantic Scholar API; it states all three findings. No PMID.
